notes.b: Water is far denser than air, so every stroke is a balance between pushing yourself forward and being held back. Four ideas explain what good technique in any stroke is trying to achieve.
points: Streamlining means making the body as slim and smooth in the water as possible: a flat, horizontal, straight body reduces resistance, so the swimmer travels further for the same effort.
Drag is the resistance the water creates against a moving body. It slows the swimmer, which is why a poor body position (for example, legs hanging low) costs speed.
Propulsion (the force that drives the swimmer forward) comes from the swimmer pushing water backwards with the hands and feet.
Newton's third law (every action has an equal and opposite reaction) explains propulsion: the backward push on the water is matched by an equal and opposite forward push on the swimmer.
notes.tip: Swimming appears in written answers on economy of movement in front crawl and on Newton's laws, so link propulsion to Newton's third law and link streamlining to reduced drag.

notes.b: Front crawl is the stroke swum face down with alternating arms and a continuous kick. The technique breaks into body position, arm action, kick, breathing and co-ordination.
points: Body position: the body is flat, which keeps it streamlined, with a slight body roll (the body rotating a little from side to side as each arm pulls).
Arm entry: the hand enters the water in front of the shoulder, fingers first, and the arm extends forward so the swimmer reaches forward and the stroke is long.

Catch and pull: the catch (the moment the hand grips the water) is made with a high elbow, so the forearm can push water backwards, and the arm pulls in an S or straight line under the body to the thigh.
Exit and recovery: the hand leaves the water at the thigh, and the arm swings forward in a relaxed, elbow-high recovery (the arm's return to the entry position).
Kick: a flutter kick (small, fast, alternating up-and-down leg beats) from the hip with relaxed ankles, so the kick stays smooth and loose.

Breathing and head: the head rotates to the side with the body roll, so the swimmer breathes without lifting the head. Breathing is bilateral (alternating sides) every three strokes, or unilateral (always the same side).
Co-ordination: usually six kicks for each arm cycle (one full pull and recovery by both arms).
notes.tip: Economy of movement in front crawl is asked about in written answers, so describe the flat body, high-elbow catch and relaxed recovery. Remember that front crawl does not need a two-handed touch at turns or the finish.

notes.b: Backstroke is swum on the back, so the swimmer can breathe freely and the main technical points are keeping the body position high and the arms working in a continuous cycle.
points: Body position: on the back, with the head still and the hips high, which keeps the body flat and streamlined.
Arm entry: the little finger enters first, in line with the shoulder, which keeps the entry straight.
Catch and pull: a bent-arm pull to the thigh.
Recovery: a straight-arm recovery over the top (the arm swings out of the water and over the swimmer to the entry point).
Kick: a flutter kick (alternating up-and-down leg beats), as in front crawl.
Breathing and head: the head stays still with the eyes up, and breathing is regular, because the face is out of the water.
Co-ordination: a body roll (the body rotating a little from side to side) accompanies the arm stroke.
notes.tip: Backstroke, like front crawl, does not require a two-handed touch at turns or the finish.

notes.b: Breaststroke is different from the other strokes because both arms and both legs move together and in the same way on each side. Its timing matters as much as the individual movements.
points: Body position: a flat body with a slight undulation (a gentle rising and falling of the body).
Catch and pull: the arms pull out and round in a heart shape.
Recovery: the arms recover (return to the start position) forward together under the water.
Kick: a whip kick, with the feet turned out, drawn up, then driven round and back. It is not a flutter kick.
Breathing and head: the swimmer breathes as the arms pull, so breathing fits into the stroke rhythm.
Co-ordination: the timing is pull, breathe, kick, glide (a short, streamlined stretch between strokes).
notes.tip: The breaststroke kick is a whip kick with the feet turned out, not a flutter kick. Breaststroke needs a simultaneous two-handed touch at turns and the finish.

notes.b: Butterfly is swum with both arms moving together and a wave-like body movement, so the body, arms and legs must be timed together.
points: Body position: the body moves in an undulating, dolphin-like movement (a wave running through the body from chest to feet).
Arm entry: both arms enter together in front of the shoulders, so the stroke stays symmetrical.
Catch and pull: the arms pull under the body in a keyhole shape (wide at the hands, narrowing under the chest, then widening again).
Recovery: the arms recover (return to the entry position) together over the water.
Kick: a dolphin kick (both legs kicking together, like a dolphin's tail).
Breathing and head: the swimmer breathes forward as the arms finish the pull.
Co-ordination: two dolphin kicks for each arm cycle (one full pull and recovery).
notes.tip: Butterfly needs a simultaneous two-handed touch at turns and the finish.

notes.b: A good start gives the swimmer speed from the first moment, so the aim is to enter the water in a streamlined shape and glide before stroking. The start differs for backstroke because that stroke begins in the water.
points: 1. Dive start (front crawl, breaststroke and butterfly): crouch on the block.
2. Drive off the block.
3. Make a streamlined entry through one point, so the whole body follows the hands through the same hole in the water and meets little drag.
4. Glide (travel forward without stroking).
5. Begin the stroke.
Backstroke start: starting in the water and holding the block, the swimmer drives back over the water.

notes.b: A turn lets the swimmer change direction at the wall without losing speed. Which turn is used depends on the stroke.
points: Tumble turn (front crawl and backstroke): a somersault at the wall, then the feet are planted against the wall.
Tumble turn: the swimmer pushes off the wall in a streamlined position, which keeps drag low.
Open turn (breaststroke and butterfly): the swimmer touches the wall with a simultaneous two-handed touch.
Backstroke flags warn the swimmer that the wall is approaching, because the swimmer cannot see the wall when on the back.
notes.tip: Breaststroke and butterfly require a simultaneous two-handed touch at turns; front crawl and backstroke do not, because they use the tumble turn.

notes.b: The finish is the last chance to win or lose time, so the swimmer keeps full speed right to the wall.
points: Touch the wall at full stretch, without slowing down.
Breaststroke and butterfly finish with a simultaneous two-handed touch (both hands touching the wall at the same time).
Front crawl and backstroke do not require a two-handed touch.
notes.tip: Remember the split: breaststroke and butterfly need two hands together at the finish; front crawl and backstroke do not.

notes.b: A short race and a long race need different technique because they draw on different energy systems (the body's ways of producing the energy for muscles). Sprinters go flat out; distance swimmers save energy.
points: Sprint: maximal effort, a faster stroke rate (more arm cycles each minute), more kicking and fewer breaths, so the swimmer keeps moving at top speed.
Sprint: the energy comes from the ATP-PC system (energy from stored ATP and phosphocreatine in the muscle) and the lactic acid system (energy made without oxygen, which produces lactic acid).
Distance: even pacing (the same speed throughout), with longer and more efficient strokes, so each stroke carries the swimmer further.
Distance: a two-beat or lighter kick (a kick that is lighter, with fewer beats for each arm cycle) saves energy, and breathing is regular, so the swimmer can keep going for longer.
Distance: the energy comes from the aerobic system (energy made using oxygen).
notes.tip: Energy systems are linked to swimming in written answers, so name the system for each event: ATP-PC and lactic acid for sprint, aerobic for distance.

notes.b: Analysing a stroke means spotting a fault and saying what causes it. Four faults are listed.
points: Sinking legs: usually caused by the head being held too high, which drops the hips and legs and makes the body less streamlined.
Crossing over at entry: the hand enters across the centre line of the body (an imaginary line down the middle of the body), rather than in front of the shoulder.
Dropping the elbow in the pull: the elbow sinks during the catch and pull (the part of the stroke where the hand grips and pulls the water).
Mistimed breathing: breathing out of time with the arm stroke breaks the rhythm, so the stroke loses speed.

keyTerms.definition: A flat, horizontal, straight body position that reduces resistance in the water.
The resistance the water creates against a moving body, which slows the swimmer.
The forward movement produced by pushing water backwards with the hands and feet.
The point in the arm pull at which the hand and forearm first grip the water.
An alternating leg kick from the hip with relaxed ankles.
A breaststroke kick in which the feet are turned out, drawn up, then driven round and back.
A kick in which the legs move together in an undulating movement, used in butterfly.
A turn in which the swimmer somersaults at the wall, plants the feet and pushes off streamlined.
A turn in which the swimmer touches the wall with a simultaneous two-handed touch, used in breaststroke and butterfly.
A start in which the swimmer crouches on the block, drives off and enters the water streamlined through one point.
Swimming at maximal effort over a short distance, with a fast stroke rate and fewer breaths.
Swimming over a long distance at an even pace, with longer and more efficient strokes.

questions.prompt: Describe the arm action and breathing in front crawl, giving key technique points.
questions.model: Arm action: the hand enters in front of the shoulder, fingers first, and the arm extends forward. The catch is made with a high elbow, and the arm pulls in an S or straight line under the body to the thigh. The hand exits the water at the thigh, and the arm recovers in a relaxed way with the elbow high. Breathing: the head rotates to the side with the body roll to take a breath. The swimmer breathes bilaterally every three strokes or unilaterally.

questions.prompt: Compare the demands of sprint and distance swimming in terms of technique and energy systems.
questions.model: Sprint swimming uses maximal effort, a faster stroke rate, more kicking and fewer breaths. Its energy comes from the ATP-PC and lactic acid systems. Distance swimming uses even pacing, with longer and more efficient strokes, and a two-beat or lighter kick to save energy. Breathing is regular. Its energy comes mainly from the aerobic system. The sprinter's technique is built around speed and power, while the distance swimmer's technique is built around economy and sustained pace.

questions.prompt: Describe a tumble turn in front crawl.
questions.model: In a tumble turn, the swimmer somersaults at the wall and plants the feet against it. The swimmer then pushes off the wall in a streamlined position, with the body straight and horizontal, ready to resume the front crawl.
